title: Peter of Saint Joseph against physical predetermination
source_text: CXXI. Id videre est apud Petrum istum a Sancto Joseph tractatus jam citati disputatione septima, quam pene totam insumit in refutanda gratiae Physica praedeterminatione. Et in idea quoque Theologiae speculativae capite illo septimo libri quarti. Ubi haec ejus est sexta Resolutio. Etsi juxta probabilem sententiam, gratia efficax realiter, & Physice voluntatem moveat & inclinet ad opus bonum, non tamen ad illud eam Physice praedeterminat. Cujus Resolutionis primam partem inde probat quod gratia efficax est motio quaedam realis in anima existens, eamque, veluti per modum cujusdam impetus impressi, ad opus bonum inclinans: quare sicut in rebus corporeis, impetus effective & realiter ad motum localem concurrit; ita proportione servata, impetus voluntati impressus ad motus spirituales, & supernaturales animae realiter cooperari debet.
pass_a_gloss: CXXI. This is to be seen in this Peter of Saint Joseph in the seventh disputation of the treatise already cited, which he spends almost wholly in refuting the Physical predetermination of grace. And also in the idea of speculative Theology in that seventh chapter of the fourth book. Where this is his sixth Resolution. Although according to the probable opinion, efficacious grace really, & Physically moves & inclines the will to the good work, yet it does not Physically predetermine it to it. The first part of which Resolution he proves from this, that efficacious grace is a certain real motion existing in the soul, and inclining it, as by the manner of a certain impressed impetus, to the good work: wherefore as in bodily things, impetus concurs effectively & really to local motion; so, proportion being kept, the impetus impressed on the will ought really to cooperate in the spiritual, & supernatural motions of the soul.
pass_b_english: Thesis CXXI. This can be seen in Peter of Saint Joseph, in the seventh disputation of the treatise already cited, which he devotes almost entirely to refuting the physical predetermination of grace, and also in the same seventh chapter of book 4 of the Idea of speculative theology. His sixth resolution there reads: 'Although, on the probable view, efficacious grace really and physically moves and inclines the will to the good work, it does not physically predetermine it to that work.'

He proves the first part of this resolution from the claim that efficacious grace is a real motion existing in the soul, inclining it to the good work after the manner of an impressed impetus. In bodies an impetus concurs effectively and really in local motion; so, by proportion, the impetus impressed on the will must really cooperate in the soul's spiritual and supernatural motions.
